Hexcrawl is one of the oldest and most compelling ways to play a 
tabletop RPG. It’s also surprisingly hard to learn from scratch. The 
rules aren’t complex. The problem is that no one has gathered the 
essentials in one place. The best writing on it is scattered across 
decades of blog posts, forum threads, and out-of-print supplements.
When I turned a game designer’s lens on hexcrawl, I found deep 
roots and clear principles, but no practical handbook that lays them 
out in one place. So I wrote one.
This is an opinionated guide. I recommend specific approaches, 
warn you about common failure modes, and tell you what I think 
works best and why, so you can adapt it to your table. Where the 
tradition disagrees with itself, I pick a side and explain why.
Whether you’re running D&D, Shadowdark, 
or anything else with a map and a taste for 
exploration, this book will work. 
System-neutral by design. You can 
read it in an evening and run your 
first hexcrawl next week.
• Matthijs

4
What is Hexcrawl Play?
A hexcrawl is a campaign structure built on three mechanical pillars: 
1. A hex grid  that maps the wilderness
2. Exploration turns  that give travel a procedure
3. Keyed locations  that reward going somewhere new
This book is written for the Game Master (GM), the person who 
builds the map, stocks it with content, and runs the game.
What makes it distinct?
The hex grid gives every location a coordinate and every journey 
a measurable distance.
Keyed hexes mean the GM preps content tied to places, not to a storyline
Each day splits into four watches: morning, afternoon, evening, night.
During each travel watch, the group runs the exploration turn:
pick a direction, check navigation, move, roll for encounters, dis-
cover keyed content, and track resources (rations, torches, gear). 
That loop is the core of hexcrawl play.
The result
Players push into unknown territory, manage their supplies, and 
discover what you’ve placed on the map. What they find depends 
entirely on where they go.
Summary:
• Hexcrawl = hex grid + exploration turns + keyed locations
• The exploration turn gives travel a repeatable procedure
• Content is tied to places on the map, not to a plotline

5
How Hexcrawl Differs from Other Styles
Hexcrawl gets confused with other exploration-focused styles.
vs. West Marches: West Marches is a social structure: rotating play-
ers, open table, player-initiated sessions. Hexcrawl is a procedural 
structure: hex grid, exploration turns, resource tracking. You can run 
a hexcrawl with a fixed group of four. The overlap is real, but they 
solve different problems.
vs. Pointcrawl: A pointcrawl connects known locations along fixed 
paths. Locations and the connections between them are the focus, 
not the terrain in between. A hexcrawl fills the space between. 
Pointcrawl is efficient. Hexcrawl rewards wandering off the trail.
vs. Traditional Campaigns: In most campaigns, travel is handwaved: 
“three days later, you arrive.” In a hexcrawl, travel IS the adventure. 
The GM shifts from storyteller to world-runner, and the exploration 
turn replaces “skip to the next scene.”
Summary:
• West Marches is a social structure built around an open table.  
 Hexcrawl is a procedural structure built around a hex grid and 
 exploration turns.
• Pointcrawl connects known points. Hexcrawl fills the space 
 between
• Traditional campaigns handwave travel. Hexcrawl makes travel  
 the main event
A Wilderness Waiting to Be Hexplored
The next chapter lays out six principles that define hexcrawl play. To-
gether, they answer the question every new hexcrawl GM asks: 
“Where do I even start?”
The short answer: with a small map, a handful of keyed hexes, and 
the willingness to let your players walk off the edge of your prep.

6
Six principles that define hexcrawl play and underpin 
everything else in the book.
You’ll learn:
1. The exploration turn as the core loop
2. How the hex grid shapes prep
3. Geographic danger
4. Information asymmetry and player roles
5. Procedural GMing
6. Radiating prep

7
1. The Journey is the Game
The exploration turn is the core procedure that guides the group 
through the landscape. Think of it like the classic combat round, 
but for travel: a repeatable sequence that creates rhythm.
Each day is divided into four watches (morning, afternoon, evening, 
night), and each watch follows a short checklist: direction, naviga-
tion, movement, encounters, keyed content, resources.
This loop is the game.
Every hex costs something: rations consumed, daylight spent, 
encounter risk taken. But every hex offers something too: a discovery, 
a shortcut, a resource, a story. 
The tension between cost and reward is what makes travel matter. 
Do we push into the swamp before nightfall or camp on dry 
ground? Follow the river or cut through the hills?
Terrain reading, weather shifts, route choices, camp placement:
these are hexcrawl’s equivalent of “I search for traps” and “I check 
the door.” I recommend keeping a visible procedure checklist on 
the table (see the reference card in chapter 3) so the exploration 
turn becomes second nature.
Failure mode: Watches that are just “roll dice, I narrate some walking.”
If there’s no decision in a watch, compress it to one sentence and 
move on.
Summary:
• The exploration turn is the core procedure: a repeatable
  sequence run each watch
• Every hex costs rations, daylight, and risk, but also offers discov- 
 eries and rewards. That tension makes choices real
• A visible checklist on the table makes the procedure automatic

8
2. The Hex Grid Structures Everything
Why hexes and not squares? Hexes keep distances honest: 
every neighbor is the same distance away, with no diagonal 
shortcuts. Navigation is intuitive, and measurement is consistent.
In this book I use standard 6-mile hexes (~10 km). You run the explo-
ration turn once per watch, not once per hex. On easy terrain, one 
watch crosses one hex. Moderate terrain (forest, hills) takes two 
watches. Hard terrain (swamp, mountains) takes three. More watches 
per hex means more resource drain and more encounter checks.
For players, distances become easy to read. “The tower is three 
hexes north” means something concrete: about 18 miles.
Summary:
• Hexes beat squares because every neighbor is equidistant, with  
 no diagonal shortcuts
• 6-mile hexes: one watch to cross on clear terrain. “Three hexes  
 north” means 18 miles
• You run the exploration turn once per watch, not once per hex

9
3. Danger is a Place on the Map
In a hexcrawl, danger is geographic, not random. It’s tied to 
specific hexes and radiates outward from safety in expanding 
rings. The ogre cave doesn’t care that the party is level 2. 
It was there before them and it’ll be there after.
You’re not tuning difficulty to the party. You’re placing threats on 
the map and letting players choose which ones to face.
The world warns players before it kills them. Bigger tracks mean a 
harder zone. Scorched trees mean something breathes fire nearby. 
A fleeing merchant says “don’t go east.” These are spatial warning 
signs. They let players make informed decisions about risk without 
the GM saying “this is too hard for you.”
I recommend sketching three zones expanding from the home base: 
safe (1-2 hexes from base), moderate (3-5 hexes), dangerous (6+). 
This gives you a pacing tool and gives players a visible gradient of risk.
Failure mode: A deadly encounter one hex from base, or uniform dan-
ger everywhere. Both kill the feeling that deeper = more dangerous.
Summary:
• Danger is geographic, in expanding rings from safety, not scaled 
 to party level
• Warning signs (tracks, scorch marks, fleeing NPCs) let players   
 choose their risk
• Sketch three zones from the home base: safe, moderate, dangerous

10

11
4. Players See the World Differently Than You Do
You see a numbered hex grid with keyed entries. Players see 
descriptions, landmarks, and the edges of their map. That gap 
between what you know and what they know is central to the 
hexcrawl experience.
Player cartography is a core activity. When a player draws the 
river they just crossed onto their map, they’re engaged at the most 
fundamental level. The map they build over weeks becomes the 
campaign’s most treasured artifact.
Player roles make the exploration turn active for everyone:
• Mapper: fills in the party’s map hex by hex as they explore,   
 recording landmarks and terrain
• Caller: declares the party’s direction and decisions each watch
• Quartermaster: tracks rations, torches, and gear consumption
• Chronicler: writes a short expedition report after each session  
 and maintains the rumor log 
I recommend assigning roles at Session Zero so every player has a 
job from the first watch. Roles can rotate between expeditions, but 
keeping them stable within a session avoids confusion.
Keep the map and notes in a shared location: a photo of the pa-
per map in the group chat, or a shared digital canvas. That way the 
group isn’t stuck if the mapper misses a session.
Failure mode: Players sitting passively, waiting for the GM to tell 
them where to go. That means they don’t have enough information 
to make choices.
Summary:
• You see the grid. Players see descriptions. That gap drives the   
 whole experience
• Player roles (mapper, caller, quartermaster, chronicler) keep 
 everyone active during travel
• Hand out a blank hex grid and colored pencils at Session Zero

12
5. The GM is a Cartographer, Not a Storyteller
Your main job in a hexcrawl is procedural, not narrative. 
You have four core activities:
Key hexes: Pick some hexes, and write a few sentences per hex
(2-4 is plenty): what’s here, what’s interesting, what’s dangerous
Build encounter tables: One per terrain type. Mix non-combat 
entries (tracks, weather, NPCs, strange sights) with creatures.
For example, a d6 plains table might include: (1) wagon tracks 
leading south, (2) dust storm cuts visibility, (3) circling vultures over 
a dead horse, (4) traveling tinker selling maps and rumor, (5) wild 
horses, skittish but tameable, (6) mounted raiders. Notice: four of 
those six aren’t combat. See chapter 5 for a full breakdown
Track time: Watches, days, rations, seasons. Time creates consequences
Run the exploration turn: Follow the procedure, describe results honestly
A good hex key is short and evocative:“Collapsed watchtower. 
Owlbear nesting in upper floor. Intact cellar with locked iron chest 
(old maps).” That’s enough. Expand at the table if players investigate.
I recommend writing keys per hex, each hex gets its own entry. 
But hexes that share a terrain type can also share an encounter 
table, which saves prep. One page of encounter tables per terrain 
type covers most of what you need.
Failure mode: Steering the party toward “your” content. If they go 
north and you prepped east, let them find what’s north. The con-
tent east will keep.
Summary:
• 4 GM activities: key hexes, build encounter tables, track time,   
 run the turn
• Hex keys should be 2-4 sentences. Expand at the table, not in prep
• One page of hex keys + one page of encounter tables per terrain  
 = 90% of prep

13
6. Start Small, Expand as They Explore
Your prep is a spotlight centered on the party’s position.
Keying density: In your starting region, key most hexes. Players will 
explore them quickly, and prepared content makes those first ses-
sions sing. As the map grows, the ratio drops.
You don’t need to key hexes the players won’t reach for weeks. Focus 
your prep on hexes along likely routes and at terrain boundaries.
Which hexes to key: Focus on hexes along likely routes and at terrain 
boundaries. A river crossing, a mountain pass, the edge of the forest: 
these are natural decision points where interesting things should live.
How much detail: A few sentences per hex. Write what’s visible, 
what’s hidden, what’s dangerous. Let play fill in the rest. If you’re 
writing more than a paragraph per hex, you’re writing too much. 
Here’s a keyed hex at the right level of detail:
• “Hex 12, Crow Marsh. Knee-deep mud, rotting boardwalk half-  
 submerged. A dead prospector clutches a hand-drawn map show- 
 ing a trail east. Stirges nest in the reeds, attracted by torchlight.”
Four sentences. What you can see, what’s hidden, what’s dangerous. 
That’s enough.
Start with a handful of destinations and a dozen smaller discoveries 
in the region around your home base. Grow outward from there as 
players explore. Chapter 5 defines these categories and shows what 
this looks like in practice.
Failure mode: Keying 200 hexes before session 1. That’s the classic 
burnout trap. Most of those hexes will never be visited.
Summary:
• Key most hexes in the starting region. As the map grows, key fewer
• Start with a handful of destinations and smaller discoveries near 
 the home base
• Trying to key everything before session 1 is the classic burnout trap.

14
Five steps from blank grid to first session.
You’ll learn:
1. Draw a hex map
2. Key your starting region
3. Build a home base
4. Seed rumors
5. Run Session Zero

15
1. Draw Your Hex Map
Start with a hex grid. For paper, search online for “hex grid PDF” 
and print one. For digital, any virtual tabletop with a hex overlay 
works. Don’t overthink the medium. A hand-drawn grid on paper 
is perfectly fine.
Assume the grid uses 6-mile hexes. At that scale, a journey across 3 
hexes on clear terrain fills a full day of travel. A 30-hex map gives 
you weeks of play.
Terrain variety matters more than map size. A 30-hex map with five 
terrain types (forest, hills, swamp, plains, river) creates more inter-
esting decisions than a huge map that’s all forest.
Each terrain type changes travel speed, encounter tables, and sur-
vival conditions, so place at least three types within two days’ travel 
of the home base.
Place natural boundaries: a mountain range that blocks easy pas-
sage, a river that must be forded or bridged, a dark forest that sig-
nals danger. These boundaries create choke points and decision 
points: “do we go around the mountains or risk the pass?”
Summary:
• Start with about 30 hexes at 6 miles each. Terrain variety 
 matters more than size
• Place at least three terrain types within two days of home base
• Natural boundaries (rivers, mountains) create interesting 
 decision points

2. Key Your Starting Region
Now populate your hexes. In your starting region, key most of 
them, with three tiers:
Figure 2: Small hex cluster showing home base at center, major loca-
tions nearby along clear routes, minor features along paths, and un-
keyed hexes at the edges behind terrain barriers like mountains and 
dense forest. Labels show three tiers with their exploration likelihood.

17
Major location: A destination players will likely seek out. They’ll 
hear about it through rumors and plan an expedition.
Example: “Hex 07, Iron Tower. Three-story stone tower, partially col-
lapsed. Signs of recent habitation: warm ashes, fresh scratches on 
the inner walls. Locked basement door. Something is living here.”
Minor feature: A discovery players may stumble on while traveling. 
It rewards exploration and connects to other hexes. 
Example: “Hex 02, Pine Barrens. Sparse pines over sandy soil. An 
abandoned camp with a locked chest containing a journal. 
Deer trails, nothing hostile.”
Unkeyed hex: Terrain the players probably won’t reach soon. No 
written entry needed. You know the terrain type from the map, 
and that’s enough. If players enter one, describe the landscape 
and roll on the encounter table.
Notice how short each entry is. Detail grows during play, not during 
prep. The worked example in chapter 6 shows a full 8-hex starting 
region built exactly this way, with encounter tables included.
See chapter 5 for a campaign kickoff checklist that walks you 
through this whole setup process step by step.
Summary:
• Major locations are destinations. Minor features reward 
 exploration. Unkeyed hexes are blank until players go there
• Each tier has a different purpose, but all fit in 2-4 sentences
• See chapter 6 for a worked example of a full starting region

18
3. Build a Home Base
Every hexcrawl starts with a safe place: a frontier town, a trad-
ing post, a fort on the edge of the wilderness. This is where every 
expedition begins and ends.
Your base should have:
• A name and some flavor, e.g. “Thornwall, a mud-brick town   
 where prospectors drink and argue”
• A few key NPCs: shopkeeper, healer, tavern keeper, rumor source
• A safe haven. The base exists to launch expeditions, not to 
 generate drama
I recommend keeping the base deliberately uninteresting as a 
destination. It’s a workshop, not a theme park. If the base is too 
compelling (political intrigue, NPC drama, side quests in town), 
players will stay there instead of exploring the map.
For players, the base is where they restock, compare notes, and 
plan the next expedition.
Summary:
• Keep the base simple and safe, a workshop, not a destination
• If the base is too interesting, players won’t leave
• The adventure is always out there, not in town

19
4. Seed Rumors and Hooks
The map is blank to the players at the start. Rumors are how 
they fill it in. I recommend tying each rumor to a specific hex on 
your GM map. The players don’t know the number, but you do.
Some examples:
• “Miners found strange carvings in the canyon walls to the east.” 
 -> Hex 06
• “A trader says there’s a ruined tower three days north, and   
 strange lights burn in its windows.” -> Hex 07
• “The old hunter claims the swamp past the river shows you visions.” 
 -> Hex 04
Deliver rumors through the world: post them on a quest board, 
spread them as gossip in the marketplace, or have a wounded
adventurer sell a secret at the healer’s. Mix true, partially true,
and misleading.
Failure mode: All rumors pointing in the same direction. If every 
lead says “go east,” you’ve given players one choice disguised as 
several. Spread rumors across the map so the party has genuine 
decisions to make.
Summary:
• Each rumor should point to a specific hex on your GM map
• Mix true, partially true, and misleading. The information game  
 matters
• Spread rumors across the map so players have genuine choices

20
5. Invite and Explain the Rules
At your Session Zero, set expectations for hexcrawl play. 
These are the key differences from a typical campaign:
• “There’s no planned route. You look at the map and decide   
 where to go.”
• “The map doesn’t care about your level. Some places will kill you. 
 The greater the risk, the greater the reward.”
• “Rations, torches, and gear are real constraints. You’ll track them.”
• “Travel isn’t downtime between adventures. The journey is the 
 adventure.”
A ready-to-use player handout is included in chapter 5. 
Customize the brackets and hand it out at Session Zero.
Help players build characters suited to the frontier. Anyone who can 
navigate, forage, scout, or survive outdoors will shine. 
Combat specialists are useful but not sufficient. 
The wilderness rewards practical skills more than raw power.
Then assign the four player roles from chapter 1: 
mapper, caller, quartermaster, and chronicler.
Give the mapper a blank hex grid and colored pencils. 
Roles can rotate between sessions.
Summary:
• Explain the core loop: gear up, head out, explore, return
• Assign player roles (mapper, caller, quartermaster, chronicler) 
 so nobody sits idle during travel
• Roles can rotate between sessions. The point is active participation

21

22
This is the core of the book. Here I walk you through running 
a hexcrawl session, step by step, from departure to return.
You’ll learn:
1. Session prep
2. Departure checklist
3. The exploration turn
4. Encounters
5. Discovery
6. Returning to base

23
1. Planning the Session
Session 1 is different. You’ve already prepped the starting region, 
so you’re ready. The first expedition begins at the home base: 
players read the rumor board, pick a direction, and head out. 
No advance planning needed.
Session 2 onward: I recommend having players declare their desti-
nation at least a day before the session. This gives you time to prep 
the right hexes without scrambling.
Ask them:
• Where do you want to go?
• What’s your goal for this trip?
• What route are you planning?
Then prep their route: review key entries, prepare one encounter table 
per terrain type the party might cross (forest, hills, swamp, etc.). These 
are shared across all hexes of that type, saving you from writing tables 
per hex. Note any world changes.
Between-session planning (maps, rumors, debate) means session 
time is spent exploring, not deciding.
Summary:
• Session 1: players pick a rumor and go. You’ve already prepped
• Session 2+: players declare their destination before the session.  
 Prep their likely route.
• They may deviate, but you’ll have the terrain and encounters   
 ready for the area
• Between-session planning (maps, rumors, debate) is part of 
 the game

24
2. Prepare the Group
At the start of the session, confirm roles and run through the 
departure checklist:
• Caller states the plan: destination, route, and goal
• Quartermaster confirms supplies: rations, torches, rope,   
 special gear
• Mapper has their map ready and reviews what they know   
 about the route
• Chronicler reviews notes from the last expedition and any   
 open leads
As GM, remind them of:
• Known dangers in the region (warning signs from previous sessions)
• Rough travel distance in days
• Weather (example: d6, where 1 = harsh, 2-3 = poor, 4-6 = fair). 
 Adjust the odds to fit your setting. Weather affects decisions, 
 not only flavor
This takes 5-10 minutes. In a hexcrawl, poor preparation can strand 
you in the wild with no food.
Summary:
• Confirm player roles (caller, quartermaster, mapper, chronicler) 
 at session start
• Run through departure: plan, supplies, known dangers, weather
• This 5-10 minute sequence sets the tone for the whole session

25
3. The Exploration Turn
Each day splits into four watches: morning, afternoon, evening, 
and night. The first three are travel watches. The night watch is 
for camp and rest. Each travel watch follows the same six steps. 
This is the core loop of hexcrawl play.
Step A: Direction
The caller declares where the party is heading: “We follow the river 
northeast” or “We push straight toward the ridge.” If the party is 
mid-hex (because the terrain takes more than one watch to cross), 
the caller confirms they’re continuing or changing course.
This is a player decision, not a GM prompt. If the caller doesn’t know 
where to go, that’s a signal: they need better information (a van-
tage point, a rumor, a scout).
Step B: Navigation
On clear terrain in clear weather, no roll is needed. The party stays 
on course. Roll only when conditions make it possible to get lost:
• Hard terrain (swamp, mountains, dense fog, night travel): 
 lost on a 1-2 (d6)
• Moderate terrain (forest, hills): lost on a 1 (d6)
• Easy terrain (plains, roads, clear weather): no roll
Use your system’s survival or wisdom check if it has one.
Otherwise, a d6 works fine.
Getting lost: When the party gets lost, they drift into a random ad-
jacent hex. Roll a d6 to pick which neighbor. The key: they don’t 
know they’re lost. You describe the terrain normally. They only real-
ize something is wrong when landmarks don’t match their map, or 
when the journey takes longer than expected. This is where the 
mapper earns their keep.

26
Step C: Movement
Daily Travel Summary (6-mile hexes, 3 travel watches per day)

The night is for camp, rest, and guard shifts. The night procedure is 
covered in Step F below.
Three watches of travel per day is the standard pace.
• If a hex takes more than one watch to cross, the party is inside  
 the hex between watches.
• They can still be encountered, they just haven’t reached the   
 other side yet. Mark their position: “halfway through the forest hex.”
• With three travel watches per day and easy terrain, a party can  
 cover three hexes (18 miles).
• In hard terrain, they might not clear a single hex. That’s the 
 resource tension: difficult terrain eats watches, which eats 
 rations, which shortens the expedition.
Step D: Encounter Check
• Roll a d6. On a 1, an encounter occurs (on a 1-2 in dangerous territory). 
 Use your terrain encounter table to determine what they meet.
• The mapper updates the party’s map with whatever they’ve   
 seen this watch: terrain, landmarks, signs of danger. Even on a  
 quiet watch, the mapper should note the terrain type in the hex  
 they’re crossing.

27
Step E: Keyed Content
If the party enters a keyed hex, describe what they find. This is 
where your prep pays off. Read your hex key and bring the loca-
tion alive.
If the hex is unkeyed, describe the terrain and atmosphere. Nothing 
specific happens unless the encounter table says otherwise. 
“Dense pine forest, the canopy blocks most of the light. You hear a 
stream somewhere to the east.”
That’s enough.
Step F: Resources
The quartermaster tracks consumption. In a classical fantasy game, 
that looks like this:
• Rations: 1 per person per day (deduct at the end of the day, 
 not per watch)
• Torches: Last 1 hour. Useful for caves and night, but not a full watch
• Lantern + oil flask: Lasts a full watch
• Special gear: Note when situational items are used up (rope left  
 behind, potion consumed, etc.)
Adapt these to your system. The specific items change, but the 
principle stays: every watch spent in the wild costs something.
If rations run out, the party must forage (costs a watch), hunt (costs 
a watch and requires a roll), or turn back. Running out of food deep 
in the wilderness is exactly the kind of crisis that makes hexcrawl 
memorable.
Then start the next watch. Return to Step A and repeat. Each watch 
follows the same six steps until the party camps for the night or 
reaches their destination.

28
The Night Watch
Night is the fourth watch. The party camps. One character keeps 
guard at a time while the others sleep, rotating through the 
night. Assume each character pulls one shift.
• Roll for encounters.The default is d6, encounter on a 1.
• Some GMs increase the odds in dangerous hexes (1-2 on a d6, 
 or even 1-3). 
Pick what fits your table. A night encounter means the lookout 
spots something first: do they wake the others, observe, or try to 
handle it alone? 
Characters woken from sleep may be groggy or unarmored. Your 
system probably has rules for this.
If nothing happens, the night passes. Describe it in one line: 
“The night is cold and quiet. Gorm’s watch passes without incident.”
Then move to the next day’s morning watch.
Camp placement matters:
• High ground gives better visibility
• A cave offers shelter but limits escape routes.
• Camping near water means refilling waterskins but also means  
 predators come to drink.
These small decisions add texture without slowing the game.

4. Encounters in the Wild
The encounter check is Step D of the exploration turn.
Here’s how to make encounters work well.
• You’re rolling a d6 each watch and triggering an encounter on a 1  
 (or 1-2 in dangerous territory)
• I recommend building encounter tables with roughly 60% non- 
 combat entries and 40% creatures or other potential conflicts
Here’s a sample d6 hills encounter table:
1. Shallow cave behind a thornbush. Inside: a scratched map on  
 the wall showing three nearby peaks.
2. Strong crosswind. Navigation check or drift one hex east.
3. Goat herder with a flock. Knows the region well, will share a   
 shortcut for 5gp or a meal.
4. Fresh rockslide blocking the pass. Half a watch to climb over,
  or detour through the valley (add one watch).
5. Griffin (1) sunning on a ledge. Will not attack unless provoked. 
 Its nest contains bones and a silver locket.
6. Orc scouts (3) on patrol. Will parley if shown strength. Ambush  
 lone travelers.

32
When an encounter triggers:
• Distance: Are they far away or right on top of you?
• Reaction: Is the creature hostile, curious, or fleeing? Roll 2d6: low 
 = hostile, mid = wary/neutral, high = friendly. If your system lacks  
 one, use this scale.
• Player choice: Do they approach, avoid, or observe?
Not every encounter is a fight. A pack of wolves might be tracking 
prey. A merchant caravan might offer news. A ruined wagon might 
hold clues to a keyed hex nearby.
Failure mode: All-combat encounter tables. If every encounter is a 
fight, the world seems one-dimensional, and players learn to avoid 
travel entirely. Variety turns hexcrawl travel into exploration instead 
of a gauntlet.
Summary:
• Build encounter tables at 60% non-combat, 40% creatures or   
 other potential conflicts
• Use reaction rolls and distance. Not every encounter is a fight
• All-combat tables teach players to avoid travel. Variety keeps   
 them exploring

33
5. Discovery and Exploration
Keyed content is Step E of the exploration turn. Here’s how to 
bring locations alive.
The best moments in a hexcrawl are when players find something 
unusual and interesting. A crumbling tower on a cliff. A cave behind 
a waterfall. A stone circle humming with energy.
Visible discoveries draw players toward them without the GM needing 
to steer. From high ground, I recommend letting players see land-
marks 2-3 hexes away: a column of smoke, a dark tower, a moun-
tain peak. This gives them reasons to change course and rewards 
climbing hills.
Hidden discoveries reward careful exploration. A buried entrance, a 
concealed path, a camouflaged camp. These require players to say 
“I search the area,” and that engagement is where hexcrawl shines.
When players reach a keyed location, bring it alive:
GM: “You crest the ridge and see it: a stone tower, three stories tall, 
the top floor collapsed. Crows circle the ruin. Fresh scratches on the 
front door frame.”
Players: “We circle it first. Any other entrances?” 
GM: “Around back, a rusted cellar hatch. And bootprints in the 
mud, heading inside.”
Some locations are a single encounter. Others fill a whole session.
Failure mode: Every discovery is a combat encounter. If finding 
things always means fighting, players stop wanting to find things. 
Mix in wonders, resources, clues, and safe discoveries.
Summary:
• High ground should let players see landmarks 2-3 hexes away
• Mix visible and hidden discoveries. Both pull players forward
• Not all discoveries should be dangerous. Wonders and clues   
 matter too

34
6. Returning to Base
Expeditions end when the party returns to base. The outbound 
journey is full of unknowns.
That’s where the big decisions live. The return covers familiar 
ground, so you have options:
•  Compress it: One encounter check for the whole journey back,  
 then narrate the arrival. Good for keeping the session moving.
• Show consequences: The party passes through hexes they’ve  
 changed. The bandits they scattered have regrouped. 
 The bridge they damaged is now impassable. The return trip   
 shows what their actions changed.
•  Surprise them: Factions and NPCs don’t stand still. A new camp 
 has appeared on the road. The safe river crossing is now   
 guarded. The world moved while they were away.
Match the approach to the moment. If the session is running long, 
compress. If the players made waves, show what changed.
As the session nears its end:
•  Ask the quartermaster to report how far they are from base and 
 how many rations they have left.
•  If they make it back: they’re safe, time passes, and their discov- 
 eries become part of the world.
•  If they don’t make it back, note where they are. Next session   
 picks up there, and resources keep ticking.
•  Encourage the chronicler to review their notes: what did they  
 find, what’s still out there, what do they want next?
Summary:
•  I suggest compressing the return: one encounter check, 
 then narrate
•  The return is when the expedition report starts forming
•  Smart retreats and early returns are valid play

37
1. Downtime Activities
When characters return to base, they can take downtime 
actions (things that happen “off-screen” between expeditions). 
Frame these as player choices, not GM assignments: 
“What does your character do this week?”
• Rest and recover: Heal injuries, cure conditions, recover from 
 exhaustion
• Resupply: Buy rations, torches, rope, special gear for the next trip
• Research: Ask around about ruins, creatures, or a region they   
 plan to visit
• Hire help: Pay for guides, porters, or guards
• Contribute to the base: Fund a new shop, build a stable, sponsor  
 a scout post. Every investment should make the next expedition  
 easier or open new routes.
For example: “Aldric spends the week asking about the dwarven 
symbols from the cave. The scholar says they mark a tomb en-
trance, and that the dwarves trapped their tombs.”
That’s one downtime action that gives the party actionable infor-
mation for their next expedition. A good rule of thumb: each char-
acter can complete one downtime task per week. Players can stay 
longer, but remind them that the world outside the gates keeps 
moving. Factions advance, weather shifts, and opportunities expire. 
The adventure is out there.
Summary:
• Frame downtime as player choices: “What does your character  
 do this week?”
• Downtime actions can yield new rumors, gear, or advantages
• Connect downtime results to the next expedition whenever possible

38
2. Resources and Gold
In a hexcrawl, gold funds the next expedition. That gives it pur-
pose beyond treasure hoarding.
The goal isn’t detailed accounting. It’s real choices about how to 
spend limited resources. Set prices so that a single expedition is af-
fordable but a long one hurts. 
A rough scale: rations cost 1gp per person per day, a porter runs 
5gp per day, a guide who knows the eastern trails costs 20gp, and a 
boat to cross the lake costs 50gp.
• Rations, porters, healing, information, and base improvements  
 should all compete for the same pool of gold.
• 40gp of copper ore from the ravine funds three days of exploration  
 or one porter for a week. That’s a real choice, not bookkeeping.
• I recommend tying gold directly to the map. Every purchase 
 should open new territory or make existing routes safer. 
• A boat lets you cross the lake instead of hiking around it, saving  
 two days.
• Cold-weather gear opens the mountain pass, and what’s up   
 there is worth the cost: rarer finds, stranger ruins, factions no one 
 else has reached.
• A hired scout knows the eastern trails.
Rations and torches are the baseline cost of movement. Gold buys 
the upgrades that change which hexes are reachable. Gold makes 
the map bigger.
Summary:
• Use a rough pricing framework: real choices, not detailed   
 accounting
• Every treasure hoard should connect to the next expedition’s   
 possibilities
• Gold buys capability (boats, porters, info), not power (magic items)

39
3. Sharing Knowledge
The shared map is where the campaign lives. After each session, 
the mapper updates it with new terrain, landmarks, dangers, 
and discoveries.
The mapper tracks the hex grid, and the chronicler (introduced in 
chapter 1) keeps expedition reports and the rumor log up to date 
after each session.
Rotate the chronicler role if writing isn’t everyone’s thing.
The shared map stays with the mapper. The chronicle stays with 
the group.
Physical map on a wall, or shared digital canvas for online play. 
Either way, the map is player-owned.
Summary:
• The mapper updates the shared map after each session. It’s   
 where the campaign lives
• Expedition reports, rumor logs, and color-coded markers keep  
 knowledge organized
• The map is player-owned, their record of the world, not yours

40
4. Factions and the Living World
The wilderness shouldn’t stand still while the players are in town. 
Factions make the hex map feel alive.
A faction is any group with a name and an agenda. You probably 
won’t need factions until a few sessions in, when the players have 
made enough noise to attract attention. When you do, keep a short 
list. For each faction, note three things: who they are, what they want, 
and one or two key figures the players might meet. For example:
• Goblins of Hex 03 (want to expand territory).
 Leader: Skrag, a cunning scout.
• Iron Road Merchants (want safe trade routes).
 Contact: Dalla, a caravan boss who pays for information.
• The Displaced Bandits (want revenge on the party).
 Leader: Harsk, a scarred veteran the players will recognize.

41
Between sessions, ask yourself: “What has changed?” 
Pick one or two things:
• The goblins have moved from Hex 03 to Hex 05, and the bridge  
 crossing is now guarded
• The Iron Road Merchants have established a camp at Hex 04,  
 bringing new rumors and trade
• The bandits the party drove off have regrouped two hexes 
 further east
As factions grow important, add them to your encounter tables. If 
the goblins control Hex 05, they should show up on that hex’s 
encounter rolls.
Failure mode: Factions that only exist in hexes the players haven’t 
been to yet. If changes never touch explored territory, they’re invisible.
This gives you everything you need to run factions. Once you’ve 
played a campaign or two, the Encounter Design Guidebook has 
more techniques for weaving factions into your encounter tables.
Summary:
• A faction needs three things: a name, an agenda, and a key figure
• Between sessions, ask “what has changed?” and update 1-2 factions
• Add important factions to encounter tables so players meet   
 them on the road

42
5. Time Keeps Moving
I recommend a default of 1 week of in-game time between 
sessions. This creates natural consequences without overwhelm-
ing bookkeeping.
That means:
• Seasons change, affecting travel speed and survival conditions
• Rumors grow old or are overtaken by events
• Enemies regroup, fortify, or move on
• New threats emerge, especially if left unchecked
Start each session with a brief update: 
“A week has passed. The first snow has fallen on the ridge. A new 
merchant arrived in Thornwall.”
This signals that the world doesn’t 
pause for them.
A loose week count 
is enough.
Summary:
• Default to 1 week of in-  
 game time between 
 sessions
• Start each session with a  
 brief “what’s changed”   
 update
• Time passing creates 
 urgency. Leads don’t   
 wait forever

43

Aldric researches the dwarven symbols from 
the cave. The scholar tells him they mark a 
tomb entrance, and the dwarves trapped 
their tombs. 
Thessa hires a porter for the next trip.

1. Essential Tools
You need three tools for Session Zero:
• Hex map with terrain types filled in (hand-drawn or digital)
• Hex key document: numbered entries, 2-4 sentences each
• Encounter tables: one per terrain type, d6 is enough to start
Once you’re running, add these as needed:
• Blank hex grid: for player mapping (physical or digital)
• Session log: A few bullet points after each game: where the

 The chronicler (chapter 1) keeps the player version. You keep   
 your own, including things the players don’t know yet.
• Rumor tracker: A simple table with three columns: the rumor,  
 where it came from, and its status. You don’t need to decide   
 whether a rumor is true when you write it. Let play settle that.

□ A handful of major locations keyed
□ A dozen minor features keyed

47
3. Session Prep Checklist
Session prep should take 30-60 minutes. If you’re spending 3+ 
hours, you might be over-keying, or you might just love world-
building. Either way, most of that detail won’t hit the table this 
session. Prep what’s on the party’s route and save the rest.
Before Prep:
• Get the players’ destination and route (before the session)
• Identify the hexes along their likely path
Prepare:
• Key unkeyed hexes on their route and prepare 2-3 encounters  
 per terrain type
• Any NPCs or creatures at their destination
• Weather and travel conditions
• Review rumors and previous discoveries
• 1-2 world changes since last session (factions, weather, events)
That’s it. Let the players fill in the rest with their choices.
Failure mode: Prepping everything the players might do. Prep what 
they said they’ll do. If they change course mid-session, improvise or 
use your encounter tables

48
4. Building Encounters
I recommend a 60/40 split: 60% non-combat, 40% creatures or 
other potential conflicts.
Here’s a sample d6 swamp encounter table:
1. Rotting boardwalk ends abruptly. An old trail marker points 
southeast, half-submerged.
2. Thick fog rolls in. Navigation check or drift one hex off course.
3. Dead birds floating in a pool. The water smells of sulfur. Some 
 thing deeper is wrong here.
4. Trapper checking snares. Knows which paths are passable this  
 season, will share for 5gp.
5. Swarm of stirges (6). Rise from the reeds when disturbed. Flee if  
 a torch is waved.
6. Lizardfolk patrol (3). Territorial but not hostile. Will trade infor-  
 mation about the swamp for metal tools.
Notice: entries 1-4 are non-combat. Entry 3 foreshadows a larger 
hazard. Entry 4 offers trade. Entries 5-6 use reaction rolls and aren’t 
automatically hostile.
Notice that entry 1 points somewhere, southeast. If players follow 
that trail marker, you need something in the next hex. When you 
write clue encounters, prep what’s at the other end, even if it’s just 
a sentence.
Each terrain type should have its own table.
Failure mode: Every entry is “d6 goblins attack.” Monotone tables 
make players dread travel instead of exploring. The tables and tech-
niques in this section will carry you through many sessions.
If you want to go deeper, the Encounter Design Guidebook covers 
layered encounters, terrain-specific.

49
5. Sample Player-Facing Document
Hand this out at Session Zero. Customize the [brackets] for your game.
“Welcome to the Hexcrawl!
You’ll explore unknown territory, discover ruins, map the frontier, 
and manage your supplies.
How it works:
• You decide where to go. Check the rumor board, review your   
 map, and pick a destination.
• The wilderness is not balanced. Some areas are deadly. Watch  
 for warning signs.
• Resources matter. Track rations, torches, and gear. Running out  
 is dangerous.
• Not every fight is winnable. Retreating is smart play, not failure.
• The world changes between sessions based on what you do   
 (and don’t do).
Player roles (rotate each session):
• Mapper: Draw the party’s map as you explore.
• Caller: Declare the party’s direction each watch.
• Quartermaster: Track rations, torches, and gear.
• Chronicler: Write a short expedition report after each session   
 and maintain the rumor log.
To start: Make a character using [RULESET]. Check the rumor 
board. Pick a direction. Head out.”

50
6. Between-Sessions Checklist
After each session, spend a few minutes updating your notes:
□ Update your hex key with anything that changed during play
□ Ask “what has changed?” and update 1-2 factions (see chapter 4)
□ Add or replace encounter table entries based on what the players did
□ Review the chronicler’s notes for threads to develop

51
7. Long-Term Campaign Tips
Hexcrawl campaigns hit specific walls. Here’s how to handle them:
When the near hexes are all explored: Re-key them. The aban-
doned camp is now occupied, the bridge has been repaired, the lair 
has new inhabitants. Factions move into cleared territory. If players 
have to travel 4+ hexes to find anything new, the early game’s 
density has disappeared.
When players stop caring about resources: Introduce terrain that 
demands specialized gear (boats for coastal hexes, cold-weather 
kits for mountains), but make what’s out there worth the cost: 
richer finds, stranger ruins, factions that can’t be reached any other 
way. If gold piles up with nothing to spend it on, the resource game 
goes slack.
When the rumor board goes stale: Faction movement generates 
new rumors automatically. Returning NPCs (merchants, refugees, 
rival adventurers) bring fresh information from off-map.
When players want to build: Let them establish forward camps, 
claim hexes, and name landmarks. A second base changes the hex 
map’s geometry, creating new frontiers.
When the starting region is fully explored: Expand the map, but 
make expansion earned. Require expensive or rare gear for exotic 
barriers, discovered entrances for underground networks. Treat the 
new region like you did at the start: a handful of major locations, 
seed rumors, let them explore.
You can expand your map for a long time with the techniques in 
this book. When you’re ready to build richer, more interconnected 
regions, The Worldbuilding Guidebook is your next step.

52
8. When Players Arrive Somewhere Strange
The exploration turn gets the party to a new place. Now what? 
A crumbling tower, a fungal grove, a camp of lizardfolk traders. 
The hex key says what’s here. Your job is to make the players 
want to interact with it.
I recommend leading with a sensory detail, not a threat. 
“The air smells like wet copper and something is singing under-
ground” does more work than “you see a cave entrance.”
The first invites questions. The second invites caution. Start with 
something that makes players curious, not defensive.
Give every creature or NPC a visible motivation. 
The ogre is dragging a dead elk toward its lair. The hermit is repair-
ing a collapsed wall and cursing. The fungal guardians pulse 
brighter when you step closer to the spore pool.
Motivation is what turns a stat block into a scene. Players can’t role-
play with “hostile creature blocks your path.” They can roleplay with 
“it’s protecting something.”
Offer three ways in: When the party arrives at a location with in-
habitants, frame three approaches:
• Talk: Who here would speak to outsiders, and what do they want?
• Trade: What do they have that the party needs, and vice versa? 
• Observe: What can the party learn by watching before engaging?
Not every location supports all three. A territorial beast has no one 
to talk to, but you can still observe it and figure out what it’s guard-
ing. A ghost might talk but can’t trade. The point is: combat is one 
option among several, and the GM should signal the others.

53
Use the reaction roll to surprise yourself: You keyed this camp as 
“hostile bandits.”
You roll reaction: 9, friendly. Now they’re friendly bandits. Why? 
Maybe they’re desperate, or maybe they recognize the party’s gear.
The reaction roll forces you out of your prep and into improvisation, 
and that’s where the best hexcrawl moments live. The scenes I 
remember most vividly are the ones where the dice contradicted 
my prep and I had to figure out why on the spot.
Connect the encounter to the map:
The lizardfolk traders know a safe route through the swamp. The 
hermit has a crude map of the ravine. The ogre’s lair contains a jour-
nal from a previous expedition. 
Every encounter in a place should point somewhere else on the hex 
map. That’s how exploration builds momentum. Each discovery 
seeds the next expedition.
Failure mode: Locations that are puzzles with one solution, or crea-
tures that exist only to be fought. If players can’t interact with a dis-
covery except through combat, you’ve designed a dungeon room, 
not a hex.
Summary:
• Lead with sensory details and visible motivations, not threats
• Offer multiple approaches: talk, trade, observe. Combat is one 
 option, not the default
• Connect every encounter to the hex map so discoveries build 
 momentum

54

gion, an expedition report template, and some closing 
thoughts.
You’ll learn:
1. A complete worked example with 7 keyed hexes and 
encounter tables
2. What an expedition report looks like
3. Final thoughts

55
1. Worked Example: The Thornwall Frontier
Here are 7 keyed hexes and 1 unkeyed hex showing what a start-
ing region actually looks like. This is enough to run 2-3 sessions.
Hex 01, Thornwall (home base). Mud-brick town on a bluff. Market 
square, the Antler & Axe tavern, Marta the healer. Prospectors drink 
and argue about what’s in the hills. Rumor board by the gate.
Hex 02, Pine Barrens (minor feature). Sparse pines over sandy soil. 
An abandoned camp with a locked chest containing a journal. Entries 
describe “something shining” in Hex 06. Deer trails, nothing hostile.
Hex 03, Winding River (minor feature). Collapsed stone bridge, 
waist-deep ford. A submerged merchant wagon holds 30gp in trade 
goods. Giant crayfish (2) nest under the bridge rubble, territorial, not 
aggressive unless disturbed.
Hex 04, Fog Hollow (minor feature). Standing stones in ankle-
deep water. Touching the central stone triggers a vision: a dark 
tower against red sky (Hex 07). Leeches drain 1 ration equivalent 
per watch spent here. Eerie, no combat.
Hex 05, Rocky Ridge (minor feature). High ground with long 
views. From the summit, players can see smoke from Thornwall, 
the river, and the dark tree line to the east. Good camp spot. 
Sheltered from weather.
Hex 06, Bone Pit (major location). Ancient fossils exposed in the 
cliff face. Giant bats roost in an overhang. Copper ore vein (valuable 
if mined). A narrow tunnel leads deeper, unkeyed, left for the GM to 
develop later.
Hex 07, Iron Tower (major location). A session-sized adventure 
site. Three-story stone tower, partially collapsed. Signs of recent 
habitation (warm ashes, fresh scratches). Locked basement door. 
Whatever is inside is left for you to decide.
Hex 08, Dark Pine Ridge (unkeyed). Dense forest, no trail. Roll on 
the forest encounter table.
Notice the variety: safe base, minor discoveries, clues pointing for-
ward, a hazard, scenic high ground, a full adventure site, and blank 
forest that’s just terrain until players make it more.

56
Thornwall Region Encounter Tables
Forest (Pine Barrens, Dark Pine Ridge): d6
1. Old campfire, still warm. Bootprints heading northeast toward  
 the ridge.
2. Deer herd crossing the trail. Quiet, undisturbed, a sign this area  
 is safe.
3. Fallen tree blocks the path. Beneath it, a leather satchel with   
 10gp and a hand-drawn map fragment showing a river crossing.
4. Wandering herbalist gathering mushrooms.  Knows the local 
 terrain. Will trade information for rations.

Final Thoughts
You now have everything you need to run 
your first hexcrawl and run it well.
The most common mistake I see is waiting 
too long to start. You don’t need 200 keyed 
hexes or custom encounter tables for every 
biome. You need a small starting region 
(around 20-30 hexes), a dozen keyed loca-
tions, a d6 encounter table, and five rumors.
Draw the map tonight. Key a few hexes. 
Write the rumors. Invite your friends.
The wilderness is waiting.
The first time a player draws a river onto 
their map and asks “what’s on the other 
side?”, you’ll know why you started.

Glossary
Caller. The player who declares the party’s direction and decisions each 
watch. One of four hexcrawl player roles.
Chronicler. The player who writes a short expedition report after each 
session and maintains the rumor log. One of four hexcrawl player roles.
Danger Zone. One of three concentric rings expanding from the home 
base: safe (1-2 hexes from base), moderate (3-5 hexes), dangerous (6+ 
hexes). A pacing tool that gives players a visible gradient of risk.
Encounter Roll. A d6 rolled each watch. On a 1 (or higher in dangerous 
territory), roll on the terrain’s encounter table.
Exploration Turn. The core hexcrawl procedure, run once per watch: di-
rection, navigation, movement, encounter check, keyed content, re-
sources (Steps A-F). To hexcrawl what the classic combat round is to a 
dungeon crawl.
Faction. Any group with a name and an agenda that moves through 
the hex map between sessions. See chapter 4.
Hex Key. A numbered entry describing what’s in a specific hex: what’s 
visible, what’s hidden, what’s dangerous. Typically 2-4 sentences.
Keyed Hex. A hex with prepared content (a location, feature, or en-
counter). In the starting region, most hexes should be keyed. The ratio 
drops as the map grows.
Major Location. A keyed hex that players will likely seek out. A destina-
tion they’ll hear about through rumors and plan an expedition to reach.
Mapper. The player who draws the party’s map, records landmarks and 
terrain. The map they build over weeks becomes the campaign’s most 
treasured artifact.

61
Minor Feature. A keyed hex that players may stumble on while travel-
ing. Rewards exploration and connects to other hexes.
Navigation Check. A d6 roll to determine if the party gets lost. Lost on 1-
2 in hard terrain (swamp, mountains), lost on 1 in moderate terrain (for-
est, hills). No roll needed on easy terrain.
OSR (Old-School Renaissance). RPGs revisiting early D&D principles 
(1974-1983), emphasizing player skill, table rulings, and emergent play. 
Examples: Old-School Essen-tials, Cairn, Knave.
Quartermaster. The player who tracks rations, torches, and gear con-
sumption. Resources create real decisions. The quartermaster makes 
them visible.
Reaction Roll. A 2d6 roll for initial NPC attitude: 2-5 = hostile, 6-8 = neu-
tral, 9-12 = friendly. From B/X D&D (Moldvay Basic, 1981). If your system 
lacks one, use this scale.
Terrain (Easy / Moderate / Hard). The three terrain categories that de-
termine travel speed. Easy (plains, roads): 1 watch per hex. Moderate (for-
est, hills): 2 watches. Hard (swamp, mountains): 3 watches.
Unkeyed Hex. A hex with no written entry. The GM knows the terrain 
type from the map and improvises if players enter one.
Watch. A 6-hour block of time. Four watches per day: morning, after-
noon, evening, night. The first three are travel watches. The night watch 
is for camp and rest.

This book gave you the foundation: the exploration turn, 
the hex map, the session loop. You can run a great hexcrawl 
with nothing else. But if you want to go deeper, the rest of 
the series is built to snap onto what you already know.
The Encounter Design Guidebook is your next step if your 
encounter tables feel thin. It covers the four encounter cate-
gories (creatures, signs, hazards and discoveries), terrain-
specific tables, faction presence in your rolls, slow threats 
that build across watches, and pacing techniques that 
make travel feel like a journey instead of a series of interrup-
tions. If you've run a few sessions and want your random 
encounters to carry more weight, start here.
The Worldbuilding Guidebook is for when your map needs 
more depth. It walks you through building terrain that 
shapes play, keying hexes at different densities, designing 
factions with territory and agendas, and layering history into 
your landscape so every ruin tells a story. If you're expanding 
beyond your starting region or building a second campaign 
from scratch, this is where the craft lives
Each book shares the same voice, the same format, and 
the same assumption: you're a busy GM who wants practical 
tools, not theory. Pick the one that solves the problem you have
